To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the neural response to a sound with simultaneous AM and FM can be characterized by a transition from phase modulation encoding (for slow FM) to a single-upper sideband response (for faster FM), with the latter response explained by the simultaneous presence of phase modulation and subsidiary amplitude modulation encoding.

1) the auditory cortex of the human brain encodes both frequency (FM, f(FM) > or = 5 Hz) and amplitude modulation (AM) simultaneously, 2) the encoding mechanism is a transition from a pure "phase modulation" response (at f(AM)) to a single-upper sideband (SSB, at frequency f(AM)+f(FM)) response, 3) this transition occurs between 5 and 10 Hz FM rate, and
the neural coding mechanism in human auditory cortex transitions from a pure phase modulation to an SSB response as the FM rate increases from 5 Hz.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the neural basis of the human auditory system, in particular, with understanding the neural coding of the acoustic features of complex natural sounds, which is essential for speech and language processing and for communication in general.
understanding the neural basis of human perception of complex natural sounds, which can be characterized by the interaction of multiple acoustic features, such as FM and AM.

the neurophysiological basis of auditory perception, in particular the neural mechanisms that underlie the processing of complex sounds, such as speech, which are characterized by specific temporal patterns of amplitude and frequency modulations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural coding of AM is a function of the FM rate.
the human auditory cortex can concurrently encode FM and AM features in a transition from phase modulation encoding to SSB encoding.
the encoding of AM and FM in human auditory cortex is a function of both the rate of the FM and the AM, with the encoding transition from phase modulation to SSB occurring at f(FM) = 5 Hz.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AM and FM features of natural sounds are encoded by different neural populations in the auditory cortex.
AM and FM features can be co-tracked by phase modulation encoding, but only for sounds with slow FM dynamics (f(AM) > or = f(FM)).

the neural encoding of AM and FM in the auditory cortex can be characterized by three distinct patterns: (1) pure phase modulation, for sounds with slow FM dynamics; (2) SSB response, for sounds with fast FM dynamics; and (3) pure AM encoding, for sounds with no FM dynamics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural coding of complex natural sounds may be more complex than previously thought, and the brain may be able to encode multiple aspects of a stimulus in a single neural representation.
the neural coding of AM-FM interactions can be investigated in humans with noninvasive methods, and that the results obtained can be compared to those from animal studies.
the neural encoding of AM and FM can be complex, and that the same neural mechanisms may be involved in both AM and FM encoding.
